entry.title: I Got Michelle Obama’s Tiny Timex
entry.summary: Timex’s Cavatina Mini is truly petite.
entry.content:
I started wearing an Apple Watch in 2022 when it came with a subscription to Future, an app-based fitness program that pairs you with a real personal trainer. My husband had already been wearing one for years, but I was resistant to something so bulky and ugly. Soon, though, I couldn’t imagine my life without one. I could monitor my workouts but also keep an eye on emails and messages without being tethered to my phone. I stopped my Future workouts but kept the watch.

Then I began to hate how beholden I was to it. It freed me of my phone but its constant pings and buzzes started to control me. I wasn’t picking up my phone as much, but I was glancing at my wrist every couple of minutes and that felt wrong, too. I also hated how constricting the silicone strap was. Plus, I could never wear a cute analog watch because the Apple Watch had trained me to become so dependent on it.

I finally swapped out my Apple Watch for the new, slimmer Oura Ring 5 a few months ago because I still wanted some biometric-tracking capabilities but in a less obtrusive form. I could now wear a regular watch, and the only one that appealed to me was a tiny Timex that we first spotted on Michelle Obama.

Timex launched the Cavatina in 1959 as its first watch exclusively made for women and recently updated its design to be even smaller than the original watch faces. Obama’s watch is the Cavatina Mini, which has a 17-mm. case — sized down from the 19-mm. Cavatina — and a brushed stainless-steel expansion band. (Strategist deputy editor Simone Kitchens tested this one.) The newest version of the Cavatini Mini comes with a leather strap, and that’s the one I called in.

It’s somehow even tinier than I imagined, but I love it more for that reason. I put it on and it literally feels like nothing. The black crocodile-grain leather strap is so narrow — not much thicker than a standard hair tie — that the adjustment holes basically take up its entire width. It doesn’t get in the way of typing on my laptop or get caught in my sleeve the way the Apple Watch did. The whole thing is delightfully retro (oval face, ’60s-script Timex logo) and understated. If I were a person who accessorized, it would be so easy to create a stack of bracelets just like Obama did with her silver baubles.

The leather watch also comes in a gold-tone case with brown strap, and, soon, in a gold-tone case with deep-red strap (available for preorder). I am also intrigued by the more classic Cavatina, which has a longer oval shape and is two mm. bigger, Roman numerals, and all-caps Timex logo. Still tiny and so wearable.

entry.summary: From a color-changing bath book to a realistic stuffed Appaloosa.
entry.content:
One-year-olds are some of my favorite people to shop for, especially as the holiday season gets going and shelves start to fill with new toys. But buying something that will bring joy into the life of a baby and that baby’s parents isn’t always easy. Do you go all-in on trendy interactive toys or err on the side of wooden Montessori heirlooms?

My son is almost 4 now, but when he was 1, his favorite toys were the ones that let him practice new skills, from opening and closing a box and recognizing common objects in his life — animals, fruit, buses — to, eventually, climbing, jumping, kicking, and learning to express himself with more complicated phrases. My favorite toys, meanwhile, were the more open-ended ones that looked nice in our apartment. Eventually, I found a balance between his tastes and my own, often thanks to the teachers, child-development professionals, tasteful fellow parents, and toy experts I called on to recommend the best toys for this age group.

Below, you’ll find more than 30 toys and books that would make fantastic Christmas and Hanukkah gifts for all the 1-year-olds in your life, organized by price, so you can browse according to your budget. entry.content:
As the Strategist’s resident tech writer, I’m always considering what gizmos I’m testing might make good gifts, so come holiday season, I’m chock-full of recommendations. But I’m just one man, and there’s a whole landscape of gadgets to try out. So I reached out to some fellow techies, as well as the Strategist’s Gen-Z expert, about the trends they’ve spotted over the past year, as well as the gadgets they’ll be recommending this holiday season.

Bella Druckman, who covers Gen-Z shopping habits for the Strategist, says that this year the gadgets Gen Z-ers used were “all about curating vibes.” Judner Aura, who goes by UrAvgConsumer on YouTube, says people are becoming more interested in creating. “Cameras and microphones are really big right now,” he says. “The low barrier to entry of social media has people inspired and driven to give it a shot.” Technology journalist Joanna Stern, who writes the New Things newsletter, spent much of this year thinking about home robots (that includes robot vacuums). There’s also been tons of buzz around the iPhone Duo, but you’d be lucky to grab one before Christmas as it’s already on back order. And, of course, the PS5 is on everyone’s list again thanks to the imminent release of Grand Theft Auto VI.

I’ve rounded up all the tech items your loved ones are most likely to ask for this holiday season, and the ones that are most likely to sell out so you can be sure to grab one. It’s worth noting that due to the RAM and storage shortages, tech items such as consoles and laptops can be in short supply and will be quite pricey this year. They’ll still make great gifts, but Aura suggests enhancing what they already have as an alternative. A good accessory goes a long way, after all.

All the perks of a modern MP3 player — including access to music-streaming apps — with hi-fi internals that make it sound better than their phone.

While many have been surprised by the return of wired earbuds, Stern wasn’t. “I’ve been using corded headphones on my computer for forever,” she says. “I just hate using Bluetooth on my computer.” These from Bose have gotten so popular that the company is having a hard time keeping them in stock.

Aura says that for those who are looking to boost the quality of their videos, an external microphone is the first step. This one from DJI is light enough to clip on their collar and has a charging case for up to 48 hours of total recording.

The latest version of JBL’s lava-lamp-like speaker features a light-up handle and a bedside lamp mode that turns this speaker into a lifestyle gadget that’ll do more than just keep the party going. But it’s great for that, too.

With this phone-size e-reader in their pocket, they’ll have no reason to not catch up on their to-be-read list. And since it runs Android, they can even install their favorite news or audiobook apps.

If they need something with a bigger screen, the aluminum version of Amazon’s latest Kindle is about as fancy as an e-reader gets.

Finally, a nice MacBook without the Apple tax.

Just in time for GTA VI. 

Nintendo’s latest console may have debuted last year, but it’s still quite popular, especially with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake that just came out.

A case that’ll ensure they always have enough juice to finish the level.

Or a more comfortable grip that’ll keep their Switch charged for hours and hours.

You don’t need to get them a full-blown console to up their gaming experience, though. This fun accessory turns their smartphone into a portable console, with consolelike controls on both sides. And since it supports Bluetooth, they can pair it with their laptop or console for wireless gaming, too.

“If I’m trying to get some quick shots on the go, this is the camera I use,” Aura says. It’s compact enough to keep in their pocket, ready to capture the moment in a pinch.

With this instant camera, every shot gets printed right away — no printer necessary.

Strategist writer Diksha Basu bought two for her kids.

Apple’s first smart display will play nice with all their other Apple gadgets and can do everything from show step-by-step recipes to managing all their home’s smart lights. And it has a great-sounding speaker, too.

Druckman says that this smart alarm clock — one of our favorites — is popular with teens thanks to its mellow design. “It’s beautiful, and a lot of teens are motivated by that,” she says. She does note, however, that it may not be suitable for college students, as she’s heard it doesn’t always play nice with college campus Wi-Fi.

“If I had a tiny kitchen with only enough space for one smart display,” Stern says, “it would have to be the Skylight. Like, there would be no arguing, my wife and nanny would agree.” It can help keep a busy household in order by showing everyone’s events, tasks, and chores in one central place. There’s even a rewards system to help keep the kids on track.

Aura just released a smaller version of its e-ink digital picture frame that makes photos look like matte prints. Images on it are truly gorgeous, and they’ll appreciate being kept in the loop with every family moment they may have missed.

Stern is also a big fan of the Matic robot vacuum. “It’s an amazing vacuum and has made incredible leaps this year in software alone,” she says. It’s true: It’s my favorite vacuum too. Its mapping is quick and all on-device, so they don’t have to worry about a map of their home ending up on some company’s servers.

Stern says the Brick was one of her most-asked-about gadgets this year. The company’s latest iteration ditches the tap-to-block method in favor of zone-based automation. Whenever they are within range of the Night — the range can be adjusted inside Brick’s app — all their most distracting apps are automatically blocked.

I tried recommending this neat little way to catch up with a friend last year, but it sold out before I could write anything about it. If they’re looking to make their calls feel a little more like the old days, I’d hop on this one quickly.

The keys on Clicks’s latest gizmo are so clicky, they’ll never want to go back to touch typing.

With this remote, they can turn the page and adjust the brightness of their e-reader, all without having to lift a finger.

Spare their hands the pain of smartphone pinkie with this luxe phone grip that doubles as a stand.

This portable charger breaks into two parts, so they can always help out a friend while keeping a little juice for themselves.

Help them up their stationery game with a printer that will let them create stickers on the fly.

It’s a Strategist classic for a reason: They won’t find an easier way to listen to in-flight movies with their favorite pair of headphones or earbuds.

Few things make as much of a statement as a phone case contoured specifically to hold their favorite lip balm.

entry.title: The 11 Very Best Air Purifiers
entry.summary: For fending off allergens, smoke, and lingering cooking smells.
entry.content:
Whether you’re seeking relief from seasonal allergies, occasional wildfire smoke, or just regular old pollution, an air purifier is a relatively affordable way to make sure the air in your home is as clean as it can be no matter what’s happening in the world outside.

At its core, an air purifier is just a fan that blows air through a filter. In fact, if you’re truly in a pinch, taping five HVAC filters to a box fan (to create what’s known as a “Corsi–Rosenthal box”) does a pretty fine job, as long as you don’t mind the noise. That’s why the most important considerations when shopping for an air purifier have more to do with day-to-day usability than pure performance. However, attributes like the pitch and tone of the fan noise, efficacy of the automatic air-quality sensors, the ease of cleaning prefilters, and how it looks in a home environment are difficult to gauge from a spec sheet. So after researching all the top-rated options available, I tested ten top-rated air purifiers and referred to previous experience with other models to find the best ones.

Updated on November 12, 2026 
The new Coway Airmega Mighty2 is our new top pick for best air purifier overall, and the original Mighty is now our pick for pet smells. I’ve also added the Windmill Air Purifier Max as a pick for people willing to pay for modernist design. The Blueair 2-in-1 Pro is our new pick for humidifying air purifiers. All other picks have been updated with the latest stock and pricing.

HEPA stands for “high efficiency particulate air,” and a HEPA filter, according to the Environmental Protection Agency, “can theoretically remove at least 99.97 percent of dust, pollen, mold, bacteria, and any airborne particles with a size of 0.3 microns (µm).” For physics reasons that aren’t worth getting into here, 0.3µm-wide particles are the most difficult to capture. So HEPA filters are actually even more effective at removing smaller particles (like viruses) and bigger ones (like pollen). “True HEPA,” “medical grade,” “H13,” and “H14” are commonly marketed terms for purifiers that have obtained independent certification for their HEPA compliance, whereas “HEPA-type” is a more misleading term meant to convey certification without having achieved it (and any model labeled as such should probably be avoided).

Clean Air Delivery Rate (CADR) is a performance standard for air purifiers developed by the Association of Home Appliance Manufacturers (AHAM) that consists of three separate tests focusing on dust, pollen, and tobacco smoke and is denominated in cubic feet per minute (CFM). These standardized tests are performed on new machines using new filters by independent labs, which means you can accurately compare ratings across certified makes and models. It’s also a requirement for any machine seeking the EPA’s Energy Star certification, and Energy Star maintains a searchable database containing CADR metrics alongside energy consumption for every certified unit across all brands.

When it comes to mitigating wildfire smoke, AHAM recommends a unit that has a Smoke CADR equal to the size of the room in square feet, which ensures that all the air in the room will pass through the filter at least 4.8 times in a given hour while the machine is running on high. For example, a 300-square-foot living room with a standard-height (eight-foot) ceiling needs an air purifier with a Smoke CADR score of 300. Because CADR is measured on the highest and loudest fan setting, it makes sense to get a unit with more power than necessary so it can still effectively clean the air while running on quieter settings.

Some brands decline to certify, citing the cost of doing so or complaints that the test de-emphasizes attributes they believe are more important than filtration speed. This feels like a cop-out. Toyota may emphasize the Prius’s fuel economy in its marketing, but that doesn’t mean they should withhold the performance figures entirely.

A machine with a built-in air sensor can keep the machine running efficiently on low when the air is already clean, only speeding things up when circumstances demand more. This saves power, keeps noise down, and extends the usable life of the filter and means you never have to worry about fiddling with the settings. While this can’t be determined on a spec sheet, some sensors are more sensitive than others and some brands will tune their auto modes to ramp up fan speeds more aggressively than others. I burned incense to test this behavior on various machines.

Some air purifiers require filter changes twice a year. Others only require annual replacement. A select few claim to last up to five years. This means that two filters that look similar and share the same sticker price may vary in actual cost by up to 1,000 percent, so it’s important to consider filter lifespan when comparing options.

“To filter both particles and gases such as volatile organic compounds (VOCs), many air purifiers contain two filters: a HEPA filter for particles and another for gases,” said Jenna Agins, assistant director of Energy and Sustainability at NYU Langone. This second filter is made from an adsorbent material, commonly activated carbon, which odor-causing VOCs stick to like iron filings to a magnet. Many filters include carbon as either a stand-alone layer or as an integrated part of the main filter. But it’s rarely enough to be an effective long-term solution. If VOC exposure is an ongoing concern, Agins recommends reducing it at the source, for example, by using only low- or no-VOC paints on interior surfaces.

A washable prefilter can trap larger air pollutants like dust and hair before they have a chance to clog up a purifier’s main HEPA filter. Some of these are made from fabric and can be thrown in with the weekly laundry; others are mesh-based inserts meant to be rinsed and/or vacuumed periodically.

HEPA: Yes | CADR Smoke: 240 | Auto mode: Yes | Filter lifespan: 1-year | Carbon filter: integrated | Washable prefilter: Yes

The Airmega Mighty2 preserves almost everything I appreciate about the original Airmega Mighty (our top pick for nearly a decade and still my pick for pet smells) while making significant improvements. It’s noticeably quieter at every fan setting and a lot more energy-efficient. It has a child lock for the control panel (that also works for pets) and a more accurate laser-based particulate sensor that distinguishes between different-sized particles while providing a live-updating Air Quality Index readout on its built-in display (in addition to the color-changing LED indicator). It also has a light sensor that automatically activates sleep-mode (turning off all displays and indicator lights) once the room lights are off for more than a minute. I used to stare at the blue glow of the older Coway’s status indicator as I drifted off, too tired to get up and do anything about it, but no more!

I’ll confess that I never cared for the original Mighty’s bulbous, chiclet styling, so the new Mighty2’s crisp edges are a welcome sight. But it’s not just for looks; the redesigned vents also help make the machine quieter. It’s virtually silent on low and noticeably quieter on high. And unlike the original Mighty, the Mighty2 never rattles or vibrates while ramping up to its highest fan speeds. On its highest setting, the Mighty2’s more efficient motor saves 18 watts compared to its predecessor (comparable to a USB-C phone charger), which should offset its higher upfront cost within a few years.

The Mighty2’s simplified filter stack is easy to clean and change. The mesh prefilter can now be slid out from the side for cleaning without taking off the front panel. A “PRE” indicator light turns on to alert you when it’s time to do this. The main filter ($70) contains both HEPA and activated carbon pellet filtration and only needs to be replaced annually. The only downside to this more integrated design is that you can’t easily replace the carbon layer with a pet- or pollen-specific filter without also swapping out the HEPA.

The Mighty2’s CADR smoke score of 240 makes it suitable for most bedrooms and smaller, apartment-sized living rooms. Its front-facing air intake vent lets you place it right up against a wall without hurting performance. (Air purifiers with cylindrical filters have higher CADR scores, but those scores are only accurate when the machine is placed far away from any walls or furniture that could impede airflow from any direction.)

HEPA: Yes | CADR Smoke: 143 | Auto mode: Yes | Filter lifespan: 1-year | Carbon filter: integrated | Washable prefilter: Yes

If you’re only planning to use the air purifier in a small room (less than 150 square feet), the Mighty2 Mini is a good option. A bigger purifier will always be more efficient and quieter (and more versatile should you ever need to move it), but $100 in upfront savings is a significant chunk of change.

True HEPA: No | CADR Smoke: 113 | Auto mode: Yes | Filter lifespan: 1 year | Carbon filter: Yes | Washable prefilter: No

If you must spend less than $100 on an air purifier, the Levoit Core 300-P is one of the most popular, highly rated items I’ve ever encountered on Amazon, with a 4.7-star rating averaged across over 100,000 reviews as of this writing. It is quite solidly constructed, features a responsive touch-control panel, and offers thoughtful features missing from other sub-$100 air purifiers, such as a child lock to prevent interference from kids and pets alike. And it’s pretty quiet compared to other units in its size range, even if it’s whinier than larger units. Its lack of auto mode and washable prefilter are acceptable trade-offs at this price, but I would personally recommend spending the extra $40 to get the more powerful Blue 511i Max in order to have those features if you can afford it.

One thing to note: Levoit stopped advertising the Core 300-P (and a few other units) as being HEPA-certified after a competitor filed a complaint to the BBB. This would give me pause if it was a new unit from an unproven brand. However, since the Levoit’s performance has been validated over the years by independent lab testing (as part of its Energy Star certification), professional reviewers, and many more user reviewers — as well as my own testing — I remain confident in its air-cleaning capabilities.

HEPA: Yes | CADR Smoke: 410 | Auto mode: Yes | Filter lifespan: 6-9 months | Carbon filter: Integrated | Washable prefilter: Yes

The Blueair Blue Pure 211i Max is about the size of a 50L kitchen trash can, and its CADR Smoke score of 410 CFM means it can quickly clean the air of rooms as large as 615 square feet on its own. This sounds like overkill for smaller homes, but headroom is nice to have on most days — because it allows the machine to run more quietly on its medium or low settings — and it’s critical in case of sudden environmental shocks (such as a nearby wildfire) when greater cleaning power is a necessity.

The Blue Pure 211i Max’s auto mode can access all fan settings and responds quickly and aggressively to changes in air quality in almost real time. Unlike most other units, which gradually increase fan speeds, it kicks into high gear at the first sign of pollution and ramps down as it’s mitigated. This makes it particularly well adapted to combined kitchen-living-dining spaces. Progress can be monitored via the numerical PM counter on top (which can be toggled between PM 1, 2.5, and 10), whereas most other units only have color-coded LEDs. While it’s audibly inoffensive when operating at a steady state, changing fan speeds does temporarily emit a whining noise that sounds kind of like a jet engine taking off.

I appreciate that the Blueair’s washable cloth prefilter wraps around the outside of the unit so you can see clearly when it’s time to launder or vacuum it. (It also comes in several colors if you get bored of gray.) The primary filter costs $70 to replace every six to nine months and consists of a HEPA filter with a layer of activated charcoal for neutralizing odors and other VOCs. For $15 more, there’s also a Smokeblock version that doubles the amount of activated charcoal, and for $20 more, there’s an Allergyblock version that carries additional allergen-specific certifications. All three are available at a 15 percent discount with free shipping if you sign up for a recurring subscription through BlueAir’s website.

It’s also noteworthy that the Blueair app is genuinely useful, and I say this as an appliance-app skeptic. In addition to tracking your home’s air quality over time, it allows you to schedule various modes to run at different times of the day (e.g., sleep mode at night and auto during the day). You can even set the machine to turn off while you’re away and turn on automatically as you approach home (although this requires sharing location data). This can help extend the filter’s lifespan, which the app calculates based on actual usage data.

HEPA: Yes | CADR Smoke: 450 | Auto mode: Yes | Filter lifespan: Up to 1 year | Carbon filter: Integrated | Washable prefilter: Yes

Blueair’s Blue Signature is one of the most powerful, quiet, and efficient models available, yet doesn’t sacrifice good design to get there. While the Scandinavian aesthetic may not suit every style of decor, I appreciate that the Blue Signature’s machine-washable cloth prefilter (which slips on and off like a tube top) can be swapped out for a variety of colors, and that its flat top allows it to double as a side table or plant stand. (There’s even the option to add a chrome plinth or wooden table legs, unavailable at the time of my review.) Other new features include a larger, motion-activated display that provides a live-updating estimate of how long it’ll take to clean your home’s air and a wraparound filter design with two additional layers of odor-reducing material. The only catch is the price, which is $100 more than the already powerful and quiet 211i Max.

Whether the Signature is worth the extra cost depends on how well it fits in your home and whether you’ll use all its new features. At 15.5 inches wide, the Signature is difficult to tuck discreetly into a corner, but if you plan to leave it in the open and use it as a side table, that extra width becomes additional usable surface area. I’ve been using it in my kitchen (in place of a 211i Max) and am finding that the additional layers of odor reduction make a difference in dispatching cooking smells that used to linger well beyond dinnertime. (I am curious to see if this is still the case after several months of consistent use.) Other features like “AirSense,” which turns the fan on high for ten to 25 minutes twice a day to refresh the air, are nice to have but only adjustable in the app. The app also lets you monitor the filter’s lifespan, which Blueair claims is up to twice as long as that of their other models. However, at $100 apiece, replacements are also $30 more expensive.

True HEPA: Yes | CADR Smoke: 286 | Auto mode: Yes | Filter lifespan: 6 months | Carbon filter: Yes | Washable prefilter: Yes

If you want an air purifier that matches your modernist decor and are willing to pay a premium, the Windmill Air Purifier Max offers great performance in a pretty package reminiscent of a fancy planter. It’s even available with a bamboo exterior. It has a front-facing air intake and can sit flush against any wall or piece of furniture. With a smoke CADR score of 286, the Windmill offers better performance than the similarly sized Coway Airmega Mighty2, and it’s comparably quiet. But at $400, with a twice-yearly filter replacement regimen at $79 per set, it costs a lot more. If they happen to be on sale for around the same price, the Windmill’s lifetime warranty (which only applies if you sign up for the filter subscription) gives it a slight edge.

True HEPA: Yes | CADR Smoke: 153 | Auto mode: Yes | Filter lifespan: 6-9 months | Carbon filter: Yes | Washable prefilter: Yes

The Blue 511i Max has most of the same features as the 211i Max, but is smaller and less powerful and uses a small color-coded LED to indicate air quality instead of a numerical display. This makes it ideal for a bedroom where space is limited and you don’t want to deal with having to activate sleep mode to get rid of any bright lights. Otherwise, it has the same responsive auto mode, washable prefilter, quiet operation, and app support as the bigger unit. Its CADR of 151 can handle most bedrooms with capacity to spare in times of need.

HEPA: Yes | CADR Smoke: 233 | Auto mode: Yes | Filter lifespan: 1-year (HEPA filter), 6 months (secondary) | Carbon filter: separate | Washable prefilter: Yes

The Coway AP-1512HH may not be the quietest, prettiest, or most powerful air purifier. But its CADR smoke score of 233 is exceptionally high for its compact size. It’s also decent in all other regards: It has an inoffensive design and it’s almost always in stock (which is important for something you might need to pick up in an emergency), and because its intake is on the front and the output vent is on top, it can be placed right up against a wall — unlike many of the columnar designs. This Coway is also one of the few popular air purifiers available with a separate secondary filter. This is helpful because adsorbent materials for trapping odors or other VOCs have a shorter service life than particulate-trapping HEPA filters. Separating these functions means more maintenance, but it also allows you to freely replace the secondary filter anytime you sense it’s starting to fade. This is especially useful if you’re using it to mitigate persistent odors, such as pet smells.

I’ve been using the AP-1512HH with a pet-specific pink filter (formulated to adsorb ammonia and hydrogen sulfide) in the room that houses my two cats’ three litter boxes. It quickly became noticeably less smelly compared to how it was with the all-in-one filter that was previously in there. This may be partly due to the aggressively tuned auto mode, which kicks into the highest fan setting within seconds of me scooping any of the three boxes. The AP-1512HH’s fan noise is a tiny bit whinier than that of our other picks and can be irksome in a living area, but I appreciate it in this context. There’s also a washable mesh prefilter for capturing dust and other larger particles.

Besides the pink filter for pets and the normal charcoal filter for odors, Coway offers a green filter for allergens and a thicker black one for intense smoke, all of which can be found in pairs at this listing for $65, packaged with a single HEPA replacement. (Cheaper imitations abound on Amazon, but using these may void your warranty.) It would be nice if these secondary filters were available separately, but that’s not currently the case.

The Coway’s auto mode responded quickly to burning incense and can access even its highest fan speeds to aggressively clean as needed. This means you can leave it in auto with the child lock activated (which is just as helpful for keeping curious cats from messing with the settings) and trust that it’s keeping your home’s air as clean as possible. Progress is indicated by a status LED that glows blue to indicate clean air, green to indicate some particulates, yellow for a lot, and red if you’re searing a steak without a range hood. While I preferred the more informative, real-time numerical displays found on some other units, it’s enough to assure you that it’s working as intended. There’s no Wi-Fi-connected app to keep track of air-quality levels over time or filter usage over time, but I didn’t miss it.

HEPA: Yes | CADR: 131 (not smoke-specific) | Auto mode: Yes | Filter lifespan: 5-years | Allergen filter: No| Washable prefilter: N/a

This Dyson unit is expensive up front, but its five-year filter lifespan and quiet operation make it a great pick for people who just want to put something in their bedrooms, set on auto mode, and not have to think about it. All you need to do is vacuum or dust the exterior every once in a while. The display on the front reports the current air quality and also maintains a color-coded log of recent readings. It’s worth noting that even with the five-year filter lifespan, it doesn’t quite pay for itself compared to a similarly powerful air purifier that requires annual or biannual filter changes, such as the Levoit or the smaller Blueair models. And its CADR of 131 is not suitable for use in larger rooms. The Hushjet’s real value comes from not having to maintain it.

HEPA: Yes | CADR Smoke: N/A | Auto mode: No | Filter lifespan: 5 years | Carbon filter: Yes | Washable prefilter: No

The AustinAir HealthMate lacks an auto mode and the sleek design of most contemporary machines — it looks like an IBM computer from the 1980s. What it does have is a whopping 15 pounds of activated charcoal and zeolite-absorbent material built into its filter. (For comparison, the entire Blue 211i Max unit weighs just 16.2 pounds.) This means the HealthMate will mitigate smells and other VOCs much more effectively and for much longer than any other machine. However, its $765 price tag is hard to swallow for all but the smelliest situations, even when you account for the filter’s five-year lifespan and pro-rated warranty.

HEPA: Yes | CADR Smoke: around 240 | Auto mode: Yes | Filter lifespan: 9-12 months | Carbon filter: No | Washable prefilter: No

This Blueair unit is not the most capable humidifier, nor is it the most powerful air purifier, but it manages to be pretty good at both functions while maintaining a relatively svelte profile (it’s only 12.5 inches wide, albeit 24.6 inches tall), so it’s a great choice for homes with limited floor space. It’s not the only humidifying air purifier, but it is the quietest I’ve tested.

The Blueair is designed to be conveniently refilled from the top — you water it like a plant and it finds its way to the removable reservoir at the bottom of the unit, which has a built-in UV light to prevent mold and bacterial growth. I also appreciated that it has an auto-dry mode for the wick that prevents it from getting funky once the 1.3-gallon reservoir is empty. The reservoir has a wide opening, making it easy to clean weekly while in use as a humidifier. Like Blueair’s other purifiers, it uses a single cylindrical HEPA filter that’s easy to replace every 9 months. The humidifying wick lasts about 12 months between replacements. You can track filter and wick lifespan and get reminders of upcoming replacements if you set the machine up with the optional, surprisingly useful Blueair app.

The machine has an LED screen on top that can display relative humidity or the current PM2.5 level in the air. Both of these stats can also be viewed in the app. The touch controls on the top front edge are responsive, and it has a child lock to prevent pets and kids from messing with the settings. I was also disappointed that Blueair doesn’t list the CADR scores for this machine in the specs. (Based on the fact that it is stronger than the previous 2-in-1 and slightly weaker than the 311i, I’m estimating a smoke CADR score of around 240.)

HEPA: Yes | CADR Smoke: N/A | Auto mode: Yes | Filter lifespan: 1 year | Carbon filter: Yes + potassium carbonate | Washable prefilter: No

If you have a gas stove and want to lower your home’s NO2 levels without opening the window, most air purifiers won’t be of much help because HEPA filters only trap particles and not gases. Filters that include a separate or integrated activated-carbon layer can be effective for a short period, but they rarely contain enough carbon to last the entire service life of the main filter. Dyson’s De-NOX HEPA filters improve performance and longevity by adding potassium carbonate. This reacts with NO2 and traps the byproducts in the filter, where they remain until it’s replaced (approximately every 12 months). Dyson claims this removes up to 50 percent more NO2 than carbon filtration alone, which aligns with the findings from a 2015 study published in the Journal of Hazardous Materials. New filter and snazzy bronze paint aside, the new De-NOX machines have the same design and pricing as the formaldehyde-eliminating models they’re replacing. Which is to say they’re very nice and very expensive.

The Dyson’s full-color OLED display is easy to read from a distance and responds to changes in air quality in real time. Its fan speed also responded noticeably quicker to any smoke or vapors emitted by my cooking in the adjoining kitchen when compared to other air purifiers. I only wish that the noise was less whiny on its highest fan settings. It’s unusable on speeds eight to ten if you also want to have a conversation in the same room.

Dyson does not believe in the value of CADR for evaluating air-purifier efficacy and therefore does not report these figures. However, Energy Star filings for similar Dyson air purifiers using similar filters indicate a flow rate of around 80 CFM for smoke. This means it is most suitable for use in a smaller bedroom or office.

entry.title: The Best Early Walmart Black Friday Deals
entry.summary: Including Dyson vacuums and LEGO sets.
entry.content:
Walmart is delivering a Black Friday double whammy this year, with an early sale beginning today and running through November 15, followed by the main event November 27 through December 1. This does seem like a lot of Black Friday, but on the bright side, here’s an opportunity to get your holiday shopping done nice and early while also picking up some pre-Thanksgiving essentials.

Because you don’t have the day off today, and therefore have time to click around an entire big-box store’s inventory, I’ve combed through the entirety of Walmart’s early Black Friday sale to find the best stuff. I spotted household appliances (like Dyson vacuums and Lavazza coffee makers), lots and lots of kids’ toys (LEGO sets, Yoto Minis), and a few nicely discounted tech items (Anker chargers, Samsung smartphones, and Beats headphones). I’ll keep updating this list as the sale continues and items come in and out of stock.

To keep in touch with all things Black Friday, read senior deals editor Sam Daly’s guide to shopping all the sales and take a look at all the products we think will go on sale this year so you can be notified when prices drop.

The sale brings some good discounts on kitchen appliances and vacuum cleaners, but also on boring household essentials like dish soap. If you’re after a new espresso machine, Dyson, or toaster oven for your child’s dorm room, now is the time.

Walmart’s tech deals so far run the gamut from Bluetooth headphones to smart TVs. The best deal is on Beats headphones, but AirPods Pro 3s are also 20 percent off.

Walmart isn’t exactly a beauty product destination, but over the years I’ve learned that its Black Friday sale is worth double-checking for La Roche-Posay products, our favorite Laneige lip treatment, Olaplex masks, and a random but pleasing selection of perfumes.

Got a lot of kids on your gift list this year? Walmart might be your one-stop shop. I’m particularly impressed with its toy deals this year: LEGO, Yoto Minis, and lots of board games are on sale. It’s also a good time to buy affordable instruments for budding young musicians.

It’s socks, jocks, and Crocs central over here. Replenish your household’s supply of slippers, bras, and pajamas, and maybe pick up a pair of discounted Hokas or Levi’s while you’re at it.

entry.title: The Very Best Kids’ Scooters
entry.summary: Including two-wheel scooters, three-wheel scooters, foldable scooters, and scooters with light-up wheels.
entry.content:
Whether they’re going around the block or just up and down the driveway, all kids can benefit from a kick scooter. (And we do mean kick scooter; electric scooters, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics, are only for those with a driver’s license.) David Jacobson at Fit Kids, a nonprofit organization that provides structured physical-activity programs for kids in underserved communities, says the best kids’ scooters help youngsters “build fitness skills, such as balance and hand-eye coordination, and when done vigorously, it provides a great cardio workout.”

In many ways, scooters are the perfect first ride-on toy: The deck is low enough to make getting on and off easy, the handlebars provide stability for new riders, and three wheels (the most common style for little-kid scooters) make learning to balance and kick at the same time less daunting. And for parents without a garage or a lot of extra space, scooters — especially those that fold up — are very convenient. They even require less space to ride on, says Chris G. Koutures, a pediatric and sports-medicine specialist at ActiveKid in Anaheim, California. Scooters can be used in smaller, more confined spaces than bicycles, making them popular among city kids who use them to zip along the sidewalk. But they’re also a great complement to a bike or balance bike since, according to Kristin Ernest, assistant professor of pediatric sports medicine at Texas Children’s Hospital, the Woodlands, scooting trains the body “differently than a bike.”

After speaking with experts and parents, here are our picks for the best kids’ scooters for kids of all ages. While in years past we’ve recommended a broader range of scooters, most of the smaller brands — bike and toy-makers who’d ventured into scooters — have since discontinued their products. We think that unless you’re looking for something specialized they don’t offer, you can’t go wrong buying a scooter from industry leaders Micro Kickboard or Razor, and if you’re looking to save a little money, you should feel comfortable buying used. Both brands offer a full range of replacement parts (Micro; Razor) should your new-to-you scooter need a refresh.

And, of course, once you’ve selected a scooter, as with any wheeled activity, make sure you grab a helmet.

Updated on November 12, 2026
We’ve confirmed availability and updated pricing for all of the scooters we recommend.

Not only is a scooter that glides smoothly over driveways and sidewalks more fun to ride, it’s a lot safer. The best scooters provide a stable ride across all kinds of surfaces, from recently poured concrete to park paths scattered with twigs and pebbles. To do that, the wheels should be made of a material that’s durable and strong enough to roll over debris without issue. In addition, you’ll want to think about wheel size: Small wheels make a scooter more agile and easier to handle, and large wheels provide more stability and speed. While wheel size varies, all of the scooters on this list have been recommended in part because of their smooth-gliding wheels.

Since kids are always growing, handlebars that can grow with them will keep you from having to buy a bigger scooter year after year. They’ll allow you to more easily pass down their scooter to a younger sibling or even share it with other kids. Look for a scooter that fits your child’s height at the lowest handlebar setting so they’ll have room to grow into the higher ones over time.

Jacobson says that a grippy deck will give kids “more confidence and better safety,” which according to him means there’s a greater likelihood that kids will spend hours riding their scooter. Some scooters have grip tape like what you’d find on a skateboard, and others have raised treads for better traction. Whatever the design, it should prevent riders from slipping if their feet are wet or if they jump on quickly. Sylvana Ward Durrett of children’s luxury retailer Maisonette considers a deck that’s wide enough for two feet an added benefit as it allows younger kids to be pulled by their grown-ups and helps new riders with balance.

A scooter should be strong enough to safely carry its rider while enduring a fair amount of abuse, yet light enough for kids to carry it. The lighter the frame, the easier it will be for your child to move and maneuver. But weight is an important factor for parents who will inevitably end up schlepping the thing in and out of the car, up and down subway steps on the way to the park or outdoor birthday parties, or all the way home if a temperamental rider has a change of heart. Take a look at the material of a scooter’s frame. Both aluminum and carbon fiber are lightweight and strong, but carbon fiber is stronger. We’ve noted the material of each scooter’s frame below.

When it comes to scooter readiness, your child’s age is less of a factor than their balance and agility: “A child who can stand on one foot, hop on one foot, and skip is probably ready,” Koutures says. First, determine if you want a two-wheeled scooter or a three-wheeled scooter with two wheels in front (for stability) and one in back. Younger kids should start with a three-wheeled scooter. Readiness for a two-wheeled scooter tends to emerge around age 6.

For older kids, choosing between a two-wheeled scooter and a three-wheeled scooter is more about the type of rider they are and how they like to steer. Two-wheeled scooters require more balance and have a “twist-to-steer” mechanism that’s similar to the handlebars on a two-wheeled bike. Three-wheeled scooters have a “lean-to-steer” mechanism that’s kind of like being on a snowboard. Three-wheeled scooters are sturdy and stable but can’t turn as sharply as two-wheeled scooters. (Micro Kickboard, maker of many of the scooters recommended below, has a helpful guide for choosing between two and three wheels for your child.)

While storing and carrying a scooter is typically easier than storing a bike by default, scooters that can be folded down when you’re not using them are extra-convenient. So if you have the choice, we’d say go for the one that folds. That said, not every scooter is foldable, and other factors might make a non-foldable model better for your child.

Handlebars: Adjustable | Traction: Raised logo on deck | Frame: Carbon fiber | Weight limit: 110 pounds | Product weight: 4.2 pounds | Wheels: 3 | Folding: No

Carrie Wren of Two Wheeling Tots recommends any scooter by Micro Kickboard because “its attention to detail, quality of design, and precision of build just can’t be beat,” she says. “No one really comes close, even though everyone tries to copy them.” All of our experts agree that Micro Kickboard scooters are strong and lightweight, glide really well across different types of terrain, and are easy for even beginners to steer. The handlebars are a cinch to adjust without tools, and there’s a foot brake on the back wheel that even very young kids can use with ease. Multiple Strategist parents have bought them for their kids and have no complaints. “It’s a stellar product and the most popular for a reason,” says senior writer Lauren Ro, whose almost-5-year-old son has now been riding the Micro Kickboard Mini for over two years.

For a scooter that’s designed for kids between 2 and 5 years old, the Mini has a surprisingly high weight limit of 110 pounds, making it very size inclusive and sturdy. (For context, the average 5-year-old weighs less than 50 pounds.) It has a two-year manufacturer’s warranty and all of its parts are replaceable, so it will last for years and is easy to hand down from sibling to sibling. Plus, if you’d like to trick out your kid’s scooter with accessories, the brand sells add-ons like bells, lights, a seat for stuffed animals, and handlebar streamers.

Handlebars: Adjustable | Traction: Raised logo on deck | Frame: Carbon fiber | Weight limit: 110 pounds | Product weight: 5.5 pounds | Wheels: 3 | Folding: No

According to Koutures, you want to “get something that a kid can grow into.” The Micro Kickboard Maxi fits that bill: A larger version of the Micro Kickboard Mini, it has many of the same features like a foot brake on the back wheel and superior steering, just scaled up for kids ages 5 to 12. As with the Mini, the Maxi’s adjustable handlebars allow it to grow with your child; they can extend ten inches (to accommodate kids between 49 and 59 inches tall), and you can raise the T-bar to any height within that range (without using any tools). It has the same 110-pound weight limit and two-year warranty as the Mini, with replaceable parts to ensure it lasts through multiple kids. (It’s also worth noting that Micro Kickboard makes a three-wheeled stroller designed for ages 8 and up, the Micro Kickboard Reloaded, that has a 220-pound weight limit, if you are looking for a three-wheel design for even older or bigger kids.)

Handlebars: Adjustable | Traction: Grip taped deck | Frame: Metal | Weight limit: 220 pounds | Product weight: 5.9 pounds | Wheels: 2 | Folding: Yes

The Micro Kickboard Sprite is a good option for kids who have the balance skills required for two-wheels — and whose parents want a scooter their kids can ride for a while. The Sprite is recommended for ages 6 and up and comes with adjustable handlebars and a weight limit of 220 pounds — enough to accommodate teens and many adults. It’s one of the lightest two-wheeled scooters on the market, and its folding T-bar and collapsible handgrips make it extra-portable (plus the brand sells a shoulder strap to make post-ride transport easier). Strategist senior editor Jen Trolio says her older daughter traded a Micro Kickboard Maxi for a Sprite at around age 7, and its smooth handling made for an easy transition from three wheels to two. For around $20 more, there’s a version of the Sprite with light-up wheels too.

Handlebars: Adjustable | Traction: Grip taped deck | Frame: Aluminum | Weight limit: 143 pounds | Product weight: 8 pounds | Wheels: 2 | Folding: Yes

For a more affordable two-wheeled scooter, the Razor A3 is constructed of lightweight yet durable aluminum with adjustable handlebars that are especially useful during growth spurts, according to Koutures. As with the Sprite, the A3’s T-bar folds down toward the kickboard, but the handle grips are stationary, making it a little less compact. It weighs about two pounds more than the Sprite and has a lower weight limit of 143 pounds.

Handlebars: Adjustable | Traction: Raised logo on deck | Frame: Carbon fiber and aluminum | Weight limit: 44 pounds for the seat, 110 pounds for the scooter | Product weight: 4.2 pounds | Wheels: 3 | Folding: No

For the youngest kids, this scooter starts out as a balance-bike-esque seated scooter with an O-shaped handlebar and a seat that adjusts to two different heights. Then it can be transformed into a standing scooter with two different handlebar shapes. The fixed-height O-bar is easier for little hands to hold, and the adjustable T-bar turns the whole thing into a scooter that is almost identical to the Micro Kickboard Mini, one of our top overall picks above.

Trolio bought a Micro Mini 3-in-1 when her younger daughter was less than a year old. It easily lasted through the next four years until Trolio handed it down to a young neighbor right before her daughter’s 5th birthday, when the same daughter upgraded to the foldable Maxi that appears in this guide. Even with the seat attached, the Mini 3-in-1 is the lightest transitional scooter we’ve found, weighing about two pounds less than the Razor Rollie below. That may not seem like much, but in the world of an 18-month-old, it makes a big difference.

Handlebars: Adjustable, removable seat | Traction: Raised logo on deck | Frame: Plastic | Weight limit: 44 pounds | Product weight: 6.4 pounds | Wheels: 3 | Folding: No

The Razor Rollie DLX comes recommended by Marissa Silva, editor-in-chief at the Toy Insider, who says its biggest selling point is that the seat can be removed easily when little kids are ready to stand up to ride. It shares this feature, as well as adjustable handlebars, with the Mini 3-in-1 above, but the Rollie’s price tag is less than half that of the Mini 3-in-1. The main trade-offs are that the Rollie is not as lightweight as the Mini 3-in-1 and has a plastic frame (instead of a carbon-fiber and aluminum one) and a lower weight limit for riders. But it does have motion-activated rainbow LED lights on the front wheels and along the kickboard, which look extra-cool when riding at sunset.

Handlebars: Adjustable | Traction: Treaded deck | Frame: Aluminum | Weight limit: 44 pounds for the seat, 110 pounds for the scooter | Product weight: 6.8 pounds | Wheels: 3 | Folding: No

Durrett loves the Globber Go-Up, which she sells at Maisonette, because of its unique configurations. It’s pricier than the other scooters we recommend, but you get a tad more versatility: It can be transformed from a push scooter to a seated scooter to a traditional stand-up kick scooter — no tools required. It’s similar to both of the transitional scooters above, but in addition to allowing riders to scoot while seated or standing, you can attach the handlebar to the back of the seat to push your kid as they ride. Trolio says this feature is excellent for very young kids who want to be independent and are very interested in scooting but may still need assistance. The seat can adjust to two different heights, the handlebars can adjust to three, and the front wheels have motion-activated LED flashing lights.

Handlebars: Adjustable | Traction: Raised logo on deck | Frame: Carbon fiber | Weight limit: 110 pounds | Product weight: 4.2 pounds | Wheels: 3 | Folding: Yes

Designed almost exactly like the non-foldable Mini Deluxe, Micro Kickboard’s foldable version takes a single click to fold the T-bar down to the deck. The age range is the same, 2 to 5, but we think spending $20 on the foldable option is a smart investment if you have younger kids who tend to tire and ask you to carry their scooter for them. Being able to fold a scooter can be a game changer, especially if you are also pushing a stroller or want to travel with it. Just like the non-foldable version, there is an adjustable T-bar that can grow with kids and an easy-to-use heel brake on the back wheel.

Handlebars: Adjustable | Traction: Raised logo on deck | Frame: Carbon fiber | Weight limit: 110 pounds | Product weight: 4.2 pounds | Wheels: 3 | Folding: Yes

This scooter is nearly identical to our best overall pick for older kids, the Micro Kickboard Maxi, with two important upgrades: motion-activated light-up wheels and a folding handlebar for portability. Trolio (whose younger daughter graduated to the Maxi Foldable LED around age 5, after using the Mini 3-in-1 since age 1) says that you can technically fold the Maxi one-handed — put your foot on the deck, then pull up on the sliding mechanism at the bottom of the T-bar to unlock the bar and fold it down. She has found this function invaluable for taking her kids’ scooters on road trips or, as suburbanites like her often do, tossing them in the trunk for trips to a nearby skate park.

The Maxi comes in several colors, has a 110-pound weight limit, and the handlebars adjust between 24 and 34 inches above the deck, meaning it can accommodate some kids all the way up to their teen years. (Micro Kickboard says it should work best for kids 5 to 12 years old.) Plus it has kid-pleasing light-up wheels, which Trolio’s daughter adored, and are especially bright and noticeable when riding at dusk.

Handlebars: Adjustable | Traction: Grip-taped deck | Frame: Aluminum | Weight limit: 220 pounds | Product weight: 9.4 pounds | Wheels: 2 | Folding: Yes

When Strategist senior editor Winnie Yang’s older daughter outgrew a Micro Kickboard three-wheeler, the big-wheel Razor A5 Lux was the obvious choice to replace it. “It’s the one she uses most, currently,” says Yang. “The bigger wheels allow it to go faster and over rougher terrain.”

With 8-inch wheels and an anodized aluminum deck that supports up to 220 pounds, the A5 Lux can support your child as they grow and even works for grown-ups trying to keep up with their scooter- or bike-equipped kids. It also folds for convenient storage or lugging with you once you’ve caught up.

entry.title: The Nothing Headphone (1) Pro Looks Great and Sounds Even Better
entry.summary: Sometimes an unconventional design pays off.
entry.content:
As I waited to board a flight in the Seattle airport, an accessibility assistant nudged me to ask about my headphones. “They’re stunning,” he said, wondering whether he should splurge and buy himself a pair. He’s right: The new Nothing Headphone (1) Pro has gorgeous transparent glass accents that flaunt the internals most headphones conceal. But I’d never recommend someone buy a $400 pair of headphones on style alone. When I told this worker they’re worth the splurge, I added that they sound just as good as they look.

“With Headphone (1) Pro, we wanted to set a new benchmark for Nothing’s audio innovation and deliver a true flagship listening experience,” a representative from Nothing’s research and development team told me. “Rather than making incremental improvements, we challenged ourselves to rethink the acoustic architecture.” That meant adopting an unusual approach, at least in terms of headphone design. Most headphones use a single-driver setup — that’s one “speaker” — to create sound. Nothing’s first premium-level headphones, on the other hand, feature three drivers, arranged as they might be in a pair of stereo speakers: There’s one for bass, another for treble, and one Nothing calls the “precision driver” that handles the midrange (which includes vocals).

While multi-driver configurations are more common in high-end in-ear monitors, where it’s hard to get even frequency response across a wide spectrum out of such tiny drivers, they’re rare on full-size headphones where a well-tuned single driver can do the trick (as it does in our pick for the best noise-canceling headphones overall, Sony’s WH-1000XM6). In fact, there have been very few full-size multi-driver headphones produced over the years, because the more drivers you introduce into a small space, the more likely you are to encounter phasing issues, wherein multiple drivers playing overlapping frequencies can cancel or overemphasize one another, resulting in unnatural (and unpleasant) sound. To minimize interference and avoid any noticeable phase cancellation problems, Nothing went through “extensive iterations of the driver placement and internal structure, combined with acoustic tuning,” before coming up with a final design, a representative said.

To our ears, Nothing’s hard work paid off: The Headphone (1) Pro has vibrant sound and a pleasantly wide soundstage. When listening to Alice in Chains’s Unplugged album, I could sense every instrument’s “placement” in the room and enjoyed hearing the texture of every guitar strum alongside Layne Staley’s haunting vocals. Even the claps and woos of the audience added depth to the track. It sounded closer to an in-person performance than I’d expect of a headphone in this price range.

Out of the box, the Pros don’t have as much low-end oomph as the Sony or Bose headphones we recommend. But that’s easily adjustable using Nothing’s surprisingly robust app. You can choose from five custom equalizer profiles: Balanced, More Bass, More Treble, More Vocals, and More Detail. You can also create a custom profile in either “simple” or “advanced” mode. Under the former, you can adjust the levels of bass, mid, and treble in relation to one another, while “advanced” mode lets you fine-tune the relative levels of the two main drivers (bass and treble) and precision driver. For those who prefer a more neutral sound, there’s also a switch on the left ear cup that enables “flat” mode, in which all processing is disabled. It’s mostly intended for mixing or producing music — they are “pro” headphones, after all — but it’s a nice inclusion that can quickly show you how much you can change the sound of the Nothings.

But Nothing didn’t stop at just making these headphones sound great. Where the company’s other headphones are mostly made of plastic, the Pro is almost all metal. The cans are made of a sturdy aluminum, while the arms are composed of titanium. Despite their mostly metal composition, though, these headphones are quite lightweight and comfortable to wear, thanks in part to particularly soft and thick padding along the ear cups and headband. Atop the cans are glass ovals that serve as windows into the headphone’s acoustic chambers; it’s sort of like looking at bookshelf speakers without grills. Some may prefer a less opinionated design, but I’m happy to wear headphones that turn their mechanical parts into a fashion statement.

The Headphone (1) Pro isn’t the first pair of Nothing headphones to impress me. The Headphone (1) and Headphone (a) both have great sound quality for their respective price points, and all the company’s headphones feature similar two-tone designs that stand out among offerings from other manufacturers. But the Pros go beyond just sounding good for their price. They sound so good I don’t want to move on to testing other headphones, and I love the look so much I wish more headphones showed off their innards. Not bad for a company’s first pair of premium headphones.

entry.title: What Dan Barber Can’t Cook Without
entry.summary: “Getting my kids to eat beets has been one of the easiest wins of my parenting life.”
entry.content:
If you’re like us, you’ve probably wondered what everyday stuff famous people add to their carts — like mascara or a sleep mask. In this iteration of our “Celebrity Shopping” column, we’re asking food-obsessed folks what they can’t cook without. Here, Dan Barber — co-owner and chef of Blue Hill at Stone Barns and founder of Row 7 Seed Company — tells us about his favorite items. As a bonus, he shared his daughters’ cooking playlist: “Cooking with my daughters to their playlist is as essential to the meal as salt and pepper,” he says.

Salt is often too salty when it’s in a fine crystal. If you taste salt, you’ve got a problem. If you’re tasting more of the food, then you’re right on the money. After 30 years of using this one, my wrist just knows how to shake it out. I can be talking to you and seasoning something. I’m not saying that because I’m a great chef; I’m saying that because I’ve done this so much. It’s like an extension of me. It’s an incredibly delicious, clear salt. It’s unadulterated.

A common thread across many of the ingredients here is subtlety. Black pepper has its place — like on a seared steak or in cacio e pepe — but putting coarse black pepper on everything is a mistake. I always tell my cooks, if the first thing a diner tastes is salt or black pepper, you’ve failed the dish. White pepper provides warmth and seasoning as a quiet backdrop. It is smoother and less aggressive and supports the primary ingredients rather than overpowering them. I use it on practically everything, alongside salt.

There aren’t better blueberries in the world than these. We’re now importing 65 percent of organic fruits and vegetables. The thing that has taken the greatest hit is organic fruits — especially blueberries — grown in soil. We’re at a point in this country where scaled commercialization of soil-grown organic blueberries is almost down to zero. Blueberries are as American as apple pie. The fact that we’re almost wholly importing the organic stuff is troubling. And most organic blueberries are grown hydroponically in a substratelike peat. Real soil gives you real flavor. These are grown in real soil. They arrive frozen, and I keep them frozen. Also, without the minerality of soil, the freezing integrity is terrible. They break down into total mush. I always have these blueberries around because you can do so much with them: savory, sweet, or snacking during the day. I’m a local guy — that’s my shtick — and sometimes I do buy local blueberries. But nobody compares to this guy’s blueberries.

I don’t know why, but I’ve always used this rice vinegar. It’s not high end. There are so many great rice vinegars out there, and I would never use this if I was highlighting rice vinegar in a recipe, like sushi rice. But when I just want it in the background, this is the go-to: very approachable, accessible, and workaday. Sometimes workaday is what you need. One of the things my kids love most that I make is a cucumber salad or a string-bean salad with rice vinegar and sesame oil. That combination is very easy and quick. I should also say that’s my wife’s recipe, not mine. The go-to dish for my kids was invented by my wife.

This is where I get into territory where I’m not going to get out without a fight. Here we go: I think the best olive oils in the world are French. I’m not an idiot — I appreciate a great Italian or Greek oil. But what I love about French oils in particular is that I don’t always want to be wowed by the olive oil. First of all, I’m in the Hudson Valley, not the Mediterranean, so using olive oil already feels a little outside my lane, and I don’t use a ton of it in my cooking. But when I do, it’s a rich source of fat that is particularly delicious as a background note to make other things taste better. I’m just not making dishes focused on raw olive oil drizzled over sliced raw fish. If I were, I’d look elsewhere in the Mediterranean. I use this everywhere because it disappears but it has a fruitiness in the background that is intoxicating. If you heat it very gently — you can’t heat it high — you get all these other flavors out of it. I often sauté lettuce very gently in this olive oil, and it tastes like a warm, fruity lettuce salad.

I love pumpkin-seed oil this time of year. It’s a rich, toasty oil that’s local. We produce a lot of pumpkins in the Northeast, and taking those seeds to make oil is a great concept. Finishing a salad, a sweet-potato dish, or squash with pumpkin-seed oil connects everything to our region. You need just a couple of drops. It’s something else.

Honestly, the difference between the best sauerkraut and average sauerkraut isn’t massive, so I’m not overly precious about the brand. But keeping it around is key. Adding a splash of the brine to cold sauces or vinaigrettes gives them an irreplaceable funk and depth, like mixing sauerkraut into braised-cabbage dishes in the fall; it adds an effortless bright tang.

Sherry vinegar has a mellow, rounded backbone without the sharp astringency of raw red- or white-wine vinegar. It wakes up a dish without announcing itself. When guests taste a dish seasoned with it, they know it tastes vibrant and complete, but they aren’t distracted by an overt vinegar hit. Sherry vinegar brings harmony. On our line, every station — from the raw bar to fish, vegetables, and meats — keeps a bottle within reach. It’s versatile enough to dress a delicate heirloom-tomato salad or finish a rich braised meat sauce.

I’ve never tasted walnuts with such rich fat and oil content. I love roasting them with a little oil and salt, then tossing them into salads and vegetable dishes. There’s also a compelling backstory: the orchard was started by Craig McNamara, the son of Robert McNamara, the secretary of Defense during the Vietnam War. Whenever I eat these walnuts — snacking on them or putting them in breakfast — I think about a son who chose a life dedicated to sustainable agriculture and nourishing people. He pours tremendous care into the land. Because it’s a smaller-scale orchard with lower yield per acre, the trees draw concentrated energy and minerals from the soil. The flavor is like a walnut times two.

Row 7 started as a seed company that grew into a produce company. We sell these incredible vegetables, and now we’re reinventing canning because the vegetables are delicious enough to hold up in a can like nothing else. These are the best beets ever invented. This beet comes from Irwin Goldman, a plant breeder in Madison, Wisconsin. His kids were embarrassed that he was a beet breeder because their friends teased them about their dad creating the vegetable kids hate most. Irwin spent ten years researching why people dislike beets. The answer is geosmin, a cluster of organic compounds that expresses intense earthiness. While adults often love that earthiness, kids are very sensitive to it. Irwin used traditional selective breeding — the kind our ancestors did thousands of years ago, with zero genetic engineering — to select for beets low in geosmin. Over a decade, he nailed it. We helped release it, and it really launched Row 7. It tastes sweet, almost like candy, with none of that dirt flavor. The flavor is so concentrated that it holds up like wine. Canning is essentially pressure cooking. In our restaurant kitchen, we can produce all fall to serve throughout the winter on our tasting menus. People who grew up in the ’70s associate canned vegetables with misery because of terrible crop genetics, poor farming practices, and overprocessing with excessive heat and time. If you start with the right genetics, grow those vegetables in mineral-rich soil, and cook them gently, canned vegetables are unbelievable. Getting my kids to eat beets has been one of the easiest wins of my parenting life.

entry.title: There Are a Lot of Great Tops at COS Right Now
entry.summary: I found so much merino wool for under $150.
entry.content:
I’ve refreshed COS’s new arrivals more times than I can count since fall started, and every batch is better than the last. The brand’s understated basics make up the bulk of my closet (including my favorite not-too-corporate black trousers). But, with all the misleading natural-fiber compositions out there, the fall 2026 collection reminded me not to overlook the line’s genuine, well-priced wools and cottons. Since COS bricks-and-mortar are few and far between outside of New York City, I tried a dozen of its newest fall (and winter) pieces to see if they feel and fit as good as they look online. Turns out, there’s plenty of great merino layers and a pair of barrel pants so good, I now have them in two colors. For reference, I’m five-foot-seven, and unless otherwise noted, I tried on tops in my usual size small and sized up from a 4 to a 6 in bottoms for a looser fit. (Heads up, I’ve found COS clothes can run a tad small.)

I embarked on my zillionth Sex and the City rewatch last month, where I was reminded of how delightful ’90s department-store knits are. This top reminds me of the mock-neck and turtleneck short-sleeves that Miranda’s especially prone to wearing. The merino is lightweight yet warm, but not overwhelming under my wool coat du jour. I enjoy the baby-tee-leaning fit but would size up for a baggier look.

You can never have enough tees. This one’s proportions are elegant: a longer bodice with three-quarter sleeves that slightly puff out, similar to the mock-neck above. The thick cuffing on the sleeves and hem are nice touches, too. It would easily pair with denim for everyday and with midi and maxi skirts for dressier callings. Simple but never boring, as I like to say.

We’re still cycling through three seasons a day in the city. This tank is a great transition option, styled as a sweater vest over a plain white tee (or on its own, as I did). The vibrant indigo-cobalt shade steals the show when worn with the neutrals in your closet. I’m especially into the fluidity of the merino, which pools and drapes around your waist; I sized up for an even slouchier fit.

I love this body-hugging long-sleeve. The merino is endlessly soft and stretchy, and the ultrafine ribbing has a smooth texture. I’m also a fan of the subtle, double-collar-looking tubular neckline and the long sleeves that cover the tops of my hands. I don’t typically wear brown, but this greige-y shade is a winner. I’ve been enjoying it as a solo sweater, but it will be handy under scratchier knits on frigid winter days.

This sweater’s got a proper double collar that does the work of layering for you. I tried it in the almost-sold-out brown-and-red color combo but am very into the other colorways, especially the white on white. This is a thicker merino wool that, without an undershirt, doesn’t irritate my sensitive skin. The wide, thick collar nicely offsets the thinner one underneath, and the V-neck is open enough that a tee underneath could peek through.

I think this sleek roll-neck is great, especially if you’re looking for something other than J.Crew’s myriad versions of its classic. Despite being labeled as a sweater, it’s more like a thick shirt. The merino’s lightweight and soft, and the cream shade isn’t sheer. I like the raglan sleeve stitching and ribbed cuffs, too.

If you haven’t already caught on, the brand’s doing a lot with the neck this season. I’m a fan of a funnel neck on a coat, and this cardigan is a handsome embodiment of that when buttoned all the way up. I can see myself dressing this up to go out for dinner on a cold night.

I was intrigued by this combination of a henley and a turtleneck. This is more suited to being an undershirt and was the thinnest of the bunch I tried. It’s made of “featherweight” wool, per the brand, and has thumbholes on the sleeves, which I associate with athletic base layers. I really enjoy the fold-over, button-up neckline and would happily recommend this as a solo top in a just-sheer-enough darker shade (the ivory was too see-through for my liking).

Speaking of henleys, this under-$50 cotton-blend jersey tee is a winner. It reminds me of the splurgier All Three one I recently wrote about with its monochrome poplin placket and buttons, two details that make it look more expensive. Three percent spandex gives it a pinch of stretch — I comfortably traveled over eight hours in it a few weeks ago — and the ribbing is so fine, it’s hardly noticeable (my preference).

I’m working on a story on white button-downs with a twist, and this menswear-inspired one is making the cut. I love the tunic length and sharp wing collar, and I can’t get enough of the French-cuffed foldback sleeves (which, when worn unfolded, are extra long and flare deliciously). I can’t wait to wear this with a red lip for holiday parties, then with loafers and jeans to the office.

I never really got in on barrel-leg pants when they first emerged. But now, I have these in white and green. Though they need to be steamed or ironed before every wear, the cotton-blend material is crisp yet fluffy. I think the invisible waist is sleek, and I really enjoy the slightly cropped 25-inch inseam. The pleats add further volume to the balloonlike, wide-fitting legs. I’m a firm believer in wearing white pants all year long, and these have just as easily paired with light tees as they have chunky knits.

I think I’ve found the hat of my dreams. It makes me feel like Mia Thermopolis in The Princess Diaries before she unveils the blowout of a lifetime. The bell-shaped cut and structure are exceptional and not as thick and clunky as other wool bucket hats I’ve found. Nor does it have too much of a brim, the issue I’ve encountered most when searching for a cloche-like hat (like this one from Soeur). The knit pattern and mid-weight merino makes for the perfect straight-on fit that hits me just at my eyebrows without obscuring my sight. And my head and ears stay genuinely warm.

entry.title: You Can Buy These Rare Noguchi Lamps for the First Time
entry.summary: For the Akari lamp’s 75th anniversary, the archival VB1 and VB3 are now available.
entry.content:
In 1986, artist Isamu Noguchi represented the United States at the Venice Biennale. Outside the U.S. pavilion, he installed a massive marble slide, a design originally conceived for playgrounds, which traveled by barge in pieces to arrive at the site. Inside the pavilion were stone sculptures, a twisting helix, and artworks Noguchi had been advised not to feature so prominently: Akari “light sculptures” — lights made of mulberry-bark paper and bamboo. The lamps held the aura of commercial products rather than of fine art (similar ones were available for purchase at a museum gift shop elsewhere in Venice), and the pavilion’s curator feared including them would incite a negative critical response. The lamps stayed.

For the Akari lamp’s 75th anniversary, two of the models that were shown in Venice are being produced for the first time since: the VB1 and VB3. Both are pyramids, a shape that Noguchi wrote “seems to be nature’s way.” They can be displayed two ways: anchored to the ground with stones tied to the base, or floating free. The stones are also covered in washi paper, a detail Noguchi credited to the manufacturer — “And, oh, what a beautiful thing!”

entry.title: My New Favorite Eyeliner Makes My Signature Cat-Eye So Easy
entry.summary: Urban Decay’s Liquid Stick is a nice upgrade to the drugstore eyeliner I wore for a decade — and a worthy replacement for a discontinued beloved.
entry.content:
My first foray into makeup, when I was about 12 years old, was picking out an eyeliner from the beauty aisle at Target. It was Covergirl’s Perfect Point Plus; I was drawn to the twist-up pencil formula, which seemed more approachable than liquid eyeliner, plus it came with a built-in foam smudger on the end. That dual-ended stick became my trusty companion as I embarked on a journey of learning how to best apply eyeliner to my monolid eyes: first as I smeared it along my bottom lash line to create a distinctly raccoonlike look (ah, seventh grade!), then, as I grew more confident, how to tightline and draw a sharper cat-eye flick along my upper lids. In the end, I was loyal to the Perfect Point Plus for over a decade.

I don’t use it as much these days since, as a beauty writer, I have an abundance of options at my fingertips, and experimenting with new products is part of the job. But when I first tested Urban Decay’s Liquid Stick eyeliner, which launched at the beginning of this year, I was struck with a pang of nostalgia. Liquid Stick is essentially a more luxe, grown-up version of the Perfect Point Plus, with some handy upgrades: It’s similarly dual-sided, with a twist-up gel-pencil formula on one end and a blending brush on the other.

But while the Perfect Point Plus has a round tip, the Liquid Stick is shaped with a slim, angled tip that makes it much easier to create a defined line. And the blending brush does a much better job than the Perfect Point Plus’s foam smudger, which would sometimes leave patchy streaks in its wake. The Liquid Stick’s packaging is also more secure; the caps on the Perfect Point Plus are smaller and flimsier and would often crack or fall off the pencil due to being jostled in my makeup bag, whereas I’ve never experienced any issues with the caps of the Liquid Stick.

Even better than the warm, fuzzy feelings it inspired in me, the Liquid Stick’s formula is comparable to another significant eyeliner in my life: the long-discontinued Marc Jacobs Beauty Fineliner. (I had high hopes that the Fineliner would be resurrected when Marc Jacobs relaunched its beauty line in June, only to find that the new Drawn This Way eyeliner is an entirely different beast altogether.) The Liquid Stick isn’t quite the same, but it’s the closest I’ve found to a decent replacement.

Both the Fineliner (RIP) and the Liquid Stick are gel-pencil formulas that glide smoothly along my lash line and impart a rich, deeply pigmented line. They also both have a precise, chiseled, squared-off tip, which I personally prefer over a round or pointed tip; after 15 years of trial and error, I’ve settled on an eyeliner style centered on a subtle flick at the outer corner of my eyes that diffuses softly into my lower lash line, and the angled shape allows me to create this look with ease. And since I have monolids, any eyeliner I apply to my upper lid needs to dry fast and remain utterly smudgeproof; the Liquid Stick is waterproof, sets very quickly, and promises up to 24 hours of wear. I’ve put it through its paces with sweaty dance-cardio workouts and emerged with my eye look totally intact. (Removal, however, takes zero elbow grease. I always do a double cleanse with an oil- and then a water-based cleanser — lately I’ve been pairing Ma:nyo’s Pure Cleansing Oil with Tata Harper’s Clarifying Cleanser — and emerge with everything fully dissolved.)

The one downside of the Liquid Stick is the price. At $26, it’s much more expensive than the $7.56 Perfect Point Plus for about the same amount of product. I’ve used the Liquid Stick pretty much every day for nearly two months and still have plenty of product left in the tube. However, since I only wear it on the outer corners of my eyes, it likely lasts longer for me than it will for anyone who lines their entire lid or who draws very thick lines. So I wouldn’t recommend it for someone who’s just learning how to do their eyeliner — start with Perfect Point Plus! But if, like me, you’re a seasoned eyeliner pro who wants to create smoky eyes, cat-eyes, and everything in between, I highly suggest giving the Liquid Stick a try.
